"Foreign election interference").[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-HighSnobiety2018-159)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-160)[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-161)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-162)[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-163)[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-164)[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-165) This has elicited responses from both industry and government to detect and limit their use.[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:21-166)[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:5-167)

In July 2023, the fact-checking company [Logically](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Logically_(company) "Logically (company)") found that the popular generative AI models [Midjourney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midjourney "Midjourney"), [DALL-E 2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DALL-E_2 "DALL-E 2") and [Stable Diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_Diffusion "Stable Diffusion") would produce plausible disinformation images when prompted to do so, such as images of [electoral fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_fraud "Electoral fraud") in the United States and Muslim women supporting India's [Hindu nationalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu_nationalist "Hindu nationalist")[Bharatiya Janata Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharatiya_Janata_Party "Bharatiya Janata Party").[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-168)[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-169)

In April 2024, a paper proposed to use [blockchain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blockchain "Blockchain") ([distributed ledger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Distributed_ledger "Distributed ledger") technology) to promote "transparency, verifiability, and decentralization in AI development and usage".[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-170)

#### Audio deepfakes

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Audio deepfakes")]

Main article: [Audio deepfake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_deepfake "Audio deepfake")

Instances of users abusing software to generate controversial statements in the vocal style of celebrities, public officials, and other famous individuals have raised ethical concerns over voice generation AI.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-171)[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-172)[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:52-173)[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-174)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-175)[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:62-176) In response, companies such as ElevenLabs have stated that they would work on mitigating potential abuse through safeguards and [identity verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Identity_document "Identity document").[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-engadget.com-177)

Concerns and fandoms have spawned from [AI-generated music](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI-generated_music "AI-generated music"). The same software used to clone voices has been used on famous musicians' voices to create songs that mimic their voices, gaining both tremendous popularity and criticism.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-178)[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-179)[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-180) Similar techniques have also been used to create improved quality or full-length versions of songs that have been leaked or have yet to be released.[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-181)

Generative AI has also been used to create new digital artist personalities, with some of these receiving enough attention to receive record deals at major labels.[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-182) The developers of these virtual artists have also faced their fair share of criticism for their personified programs, including backlash for "dehumanizing" an artform, and also creating artists which create unrealistic or immoral appeals to their audiences.[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-183)

### Illegal imagery

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Illegal imagery")]

Main article: [Child pornography §Artificially generated or simulated imagery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_pornography#Artificially_generated_or_simulated_imagery "Child pornography")

Many websites that allow [explicit AI generated images or videos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_pornography "AI pornography") have been created,[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-184) and this has been used to create illegal content, such as [rape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rape_pornography "Rape pornography"), [child sexual abuse material](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Child_sexual_abuse_material "Child sexual abuse material"),[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-185)[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-186)[necrophilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necrophilia "Necrophilia"), and [zoophilia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zoophilia "Zoophilia").

### Cybercrime

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=28 "Edit section: Cybercrime")]

Generative AI's ability to create realistic fake content has been exploited in numerous types of cybercrime, including [phishing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phishing "Phishing") scams.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-187)[Deepfake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deepfake "Deepfake") video and audio have been used to create disinformation and fraud. In 2020, former Google [click fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Click_fraud "Click fraud") czar [Shuman Ghosemajumder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shuman_Ghosemajumder "Shuman Ghosemajumder") argued that once deepfake videos become perfectly realistic, they would stop appearing remarkable to viewers, potentially leading to uncritical acceptance of false information.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-188) Additionally, [large language models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model "Large language model") and other forms of text-generation AI have been used to create fake reviews of [e-commerce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E-commerce "E-commerce") websites to boost ratings.[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-189) Cybercriminals have created large language models focused on fraud, including WormGPT and FraudGPT.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-190)

A 2023 study showed that generative AI can be vulnerable to jailbreaks, [reverse psychology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reverse_psychology "Reverse psychology") and [prompt injection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prompt_injection "Prompt injection") attacks, enabling attackers to obtain help with harmful requests, such as for crafting [social engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_engineering_(security) "Social engineering (security)") and [phishing attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phishing "Phishing").[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-191) Additionally, other researchers have demonstrated that open-source models can be [fine-tuned](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine-tuning_(deep_learning) "Fine-tuning (deep learning)") to remove their safety restrictions at low cost.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-192)

### Information laundering

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=29 "Edit section: Information laundering")]

Generative AI has been noted for its use by [state-sponsored propaganda campaigns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State-sponsored_Internet_propaganda "State-sponsored Internet propaganda") in [information laundering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_laundering "Information laundering"). According to a 2025 report by [Graphika](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graphika "Graphika"), generative AI is used to launder articles from Chinese [state media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_media "State media") such as [China Global Television Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_Global_Television_Network "China Global Television Network") through various social media sites in an attempt to disguise the articles' origin.[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:53-193)

### Reliance on industry giants

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Reliance on industry giants")]

Training [frontier AI models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frontier_model "Frontier model") requires an enormous amount of computing power. Usually only [Big Tech](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Tech "Big Tech") companies have the financial resources to make such investments. Smaller start-ups such as [Cohere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohere "Cohere") and [OpenAI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OpenAI "OpenAI") end up buying access to [data centers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_centers "Data centers") from [Google](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Google "Google") and [Microsoft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Microsoft "Microsoft") respectively.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-194)

### Energy and environment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: Energy and environment")]

Main article: [Environmental impacts of artificial intelligence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_impacts_of_artificial_intelligence "Environmental impacts of artificial intelligence")

AI has a significant carbon footprint due to growing energy consumption from both training and usage.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:82-139)[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:14-140) Scientists and journalists have expressed concerns about the environmental impact that the development and deployment of generative models are having: high CO 2 emissions,[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:1-195)[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:2-196)[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:7-197) large amounts of freshwater used for data centers,[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:8-198)[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:9-199) and high amounts of electricity usage.[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:2-196)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:10-200)[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:11-201) There is also concern that these impacts may increase as these models are incorporated into widely used search engines such as Google Search and Bing,[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:10-200) as [chatbots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chatbot "Chatbot") and other applications become more popular,[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:9-199)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:10-200) and as models need to be retrained.[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:10-200)

The carbon footprint of generative AI globally is estimated to be growing steadily, with potential annual emissions ranging from 18.21 to 245.94 million tons of CO 2 by 2035,[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-202) with the highest estimates for 2035 nearing the impact of the United States [beef industry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beef_industry "Beef industry") on emissions (currently estimated to emit 257.5 million tons annually as of 2024).[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-203)

Proposed mitigation strategies include factoring potential environmental costs prior to model development or data collection,[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:1-195) increasing efficiency of data centers to reduce electricity/energy usage,[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:7-197)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:10-200)[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:11-201) building more efficient [machine learning models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_learning "Machine learning"),[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:2-196)[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:8-198)[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:9-199) minimizing the number of times that models need to be retrained,[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:7-197) developing a government-directed framework for auditing the environmental impact of these models,[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:7-197)[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:8-198) regulating for transparency of these models,[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:7-197) regulating their energy and water usage,[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:8-198) encouraging researchers to publish data on their models' carbon footprint,[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:7-197)[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:10-200) and increasing the number of subject matter experts who understand both machine learning and climate science.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:7-197)

### Content quality

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=32 "Edit section: Content quality")]

See also: [AI slop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_slop "AI slop") and [Dead Internet theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dead_Internet_theory "Dead Internet theory")

_[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ defines [slop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AI_slop "AI slop") as analogous to [spam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spamming "Spamming"): "shoddy or unwanted A.I. content in social media, art, books, and ... in search results."[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-204) Journalists have expressed concerns about the scale of low-quality generated content with respect to social media content moderation,[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:12-205) the monetary incentives from social media companies to spread such content,[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:12-205)[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:13-206) false political messaging,[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-:13-206) spamming of scientific research paper submissions,[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-207) increased time and effort to find higher quality or desired content on the Internet,[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-208) the indexing of generated content by search engines,[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-209) and on journalism itself.[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-210)

A paper published by researchers at Amazon Web Services AI Labs found that over 57% of sentences from a sample of over 6 billion sentences from [Common Crawl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common_Crawl "Common Crawl"), a snapshot of web pages, were [machine translated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Machine_translation "Machine translation"). Many of these automated translations were seen as lower quality, especially for sentences that were translated into at least three languages. Many lower-resource languages (ex. [Wolof](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolof_language "Wolof language"), [Xhosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xhosa_language "Xhosa language")) were translated across more languages than higher-resource languages (ex. English, French).[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-211)[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-212)

In September 2024, [Robyn Speer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_Mind_Common_Sense "Open Mind Common Sense"), the author of wordfreq, an open source database that calculated word frequencies based on text from the Internet, announced that she had stopped updating the data for several reasons: high costs for obtaining data from [Reddit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reddit "Reddit") and [Twitter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitter "Twitter"), excessive focus on generative AI compared to other methods in the [natural language processing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natural_language_processing "Natural language processing") community, and that "generative AI has polluted the data".[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-213)

The adoption of generative AI tools led to an explosion of AI-generated content across multiple domains. A study from [University College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_College_London "University College London") estimated that in 2023, more than 60,000 scholarly articles—over 1% of all publications—were likely written with LLM assistance.[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-214) According to [Stanford University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stanford_University "Stanford University")'s Institute for Human-Centered AI, approximately 17.5% of newly published computer science papers and 16.9% of peer review text now incorporate content generated by LLMs.[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-215) Many academic disciplines have concerns about the factual reliability of academic content generated by AI.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-216)

Visual content follows a similar trend. Since the launch of [DALL-E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DALL-E "DALL-E") 2 in 2022, it is estimated that an average of 34 million images have been created daily. As of August 2023, more than 15 billion images had been generated using text-to-image algorithms, with 80% of these created by models based on [Stable Diffusion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_Diffusion "Stable Diffusion").[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-217)

If AI-generated content is included in new data crawls from the Internet for additional training of AI models, defects in the resulting models may occur.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-218) Training an AI model exclusively on the output of another AI model produces a lower-quality model. Repeating this process, where each new model is trained on the previous model's output, leads to progressive degradation and eventually results in a "[model collapse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Model_collapse "Model collapse")" after multiple iterations.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-219) Tests have been conducted with pattern recognition of handwritten letters and with pictures of human faces.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-220) As a consequence, the value of data collected from genuine human interactions with systems may become increasingly valuable in the presence of LLM-generated content in data crawled from the Internet.

On the other side, [synthetic data](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Synthetic_data "Synthetic data") is often used as an alternative to data produced by real-world events. Such data can be deployed to validate mathematical models and to train machine learning models while preserving user privacy,[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-221) including for structured data.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-222) The approach is not limited to text generation; image generation has been employed to train computer vision models.[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-223)

### Misuse in journalism

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=33 "Edit section: Misuse in journalism")]

See also: [Automated journalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automated_journalism "Automated journalism") and [List of fake news websites §Generative AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_fake_news_websites#Generative_AI "List of fake news websites")

Generative AI's potential to generate a large amount of content with little effort is also affecting journalism.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-224) In January 2023, _[Futurism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Futurism\_(website) "Futurism (website)")_ broke the story that [CNET](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CNET "CNET") had been using an undisclosed internal AI tool to write at least 77 of its stories; after the news broke, CNET posted corrections to 41 of the stories.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-225) In April 2023, _Die Aktuelle_ published an AI-generated fake interview of [Michael Schumacher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Schumacher "Michael Schumacher").[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-226) In May 2024, _Futurism_ noted that a content management system video by AdVon Commerce, which had used generative AI to produce articles for many of the aforementioned outlets, appeared to show that they "had produced tens of thousands of articles for more than 150 publishers."[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-227) In 2025, a report from the American Sunlight Project stated that [Pravda network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pravda_network "Pravda network") was publishing as many as 10,000 articles a day, and concluded that much of this content aimed to push Russian narratives into [large language models](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_language_model "Large language model") through their training data.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-228)

In June 2024, [Reuters Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reuters_Institute "Reuters Institute") published its _Digital News Report for 2024_. In a survey of people in America and Europe, Reuters Institute reports that 52% and 47% respectively are uncomfortable with news produced by "mostly AI with some human oversight", and 23% and 15% respectively report being comfortable. 42% of Americans and 33% of Europeans reported that they were comfortable with news produced by "mainly human with some help from AI". The results of global surveys reported that people were more uncomfortable with news topics including politics (46%), crime (43%), and local news (37%) produced by AI than other news topics.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-229)

Detection and awareness
-----------------------

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Generative_artificial_intelligence&action=edit&section=34 "Edit section: Detection and awareness")]

See also: [Artificial intelligence content detection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_intelligence_content_detection "Artificial intelligence content detection")

Online users have falsely assumed media of using generative artificial intelligence for content, such as video games _Little Droid_ and _[Catly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catly "Catly")_.[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-230)

Due to various concerns about citizens' unknowingly consuming generative AI media content, proponents argue for labeling such content to provide context. The [Cyberspace Administration of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyberspace_Administration_of_China "Cyberspace Administration of China") issued rules obligating service providers to labeling this content online.[[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-231)

The popularity of ChatGPT caused the emergence of tools that detect whether content was AI-generated, such as [GPTZero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GPTZero "GPTZero"), but the risk of false accusations ([false positives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_positives_and_false_negatives "False positives and false negatives")) has remained a concern.[[232]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-232)[Digital watermarking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Digital_watermarking "Digital watermarking") allows to reach high detection accuracy by subtly altering the generated content in a way that can be detected by software, but without being noticeable by users. OpenAI developed in 2023 a digital watermarking tool that allowed to detect content generated by [ChatGPT](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ChatGPT "ChatGPT") with an estimated accuracy of 99.9%, when given enough text. But OpenAI chose not to release it, worrying that users would switch to competitor products, and arguing that digital watermarking can be circumvented by bad actors, for example with superficial rephrasing.[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-233)[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-234) Google's digital watermarking tool called SynthID was integrated in 2025 into products like Gemini, Imagen and Veo. Google also created the portal SynthID detector for users to check whether text, images or videos were produced with Google's generative AI products.[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_artificial_intelligence#cite_note-235)

Less than five years ago, machine learning was one of the predominant ways businesses were using artificial intelligence. In April 2021,[we called machine learning](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/machine-learning-explained) a “pervasive and powerful form of AI … changing every industry.”

But after ChatGPT-3.5 was released in 2022, many organizations shifted focus to a subfield of AI, generative AI, which can be used to create new content. Generative AI _is_ machine learning (more on that below).

Traditional machine learning is now an established technology in many organizations, and today leading firms are focusing on use cases for generative AI.In a 2024 survey of senior data leaders,[64% of respondents](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/62adf3ca029a6808a6c5be30/t/66635b1a6aeebf254874237b/1717787418584/DataAI-ExecutiveLeadershipSurveyFinalAsset.pdf) said that generative AI has the potential to be the most transformative technology in a generation.

While generative AI is widely accessible and has many novel applications, you still need to know when it’s best to turn to other forms of AI, like traditional machine learning.

We talked with two MIT Sloan AI experts — associate professor Swati Gupta and professor of the practice Rama Ramakrishnan — about where generative AI is replacing predictive machine learning, when machine learning is still the most effective tool, and how businesses are using the technologies together.

**What is machine learning?**
-----------------------------

**Machine learning** is a type of artificial intelligence that enables computers to learn without explicitly being programmed. Where traditional computing requires people to create programs that give machines detailed instructions on what steps to take to complete a task, machine learning programs can learn from examples.

Machine learning is used for many purposes, from predicting customer behavior to assessing potential fraud in bank transactions to creating tailored search results on shopping sites.

The data used to fuel machine learning — including generative AI tools —can be numbers in a spreadsheet, text, images, audio, or video. The more data a machine learning model is trained on, the more accurate the model will be. For machine learning to work, there must be patterns within the data that the application can identify and analyze.

“The basic idea of machine learning is, it’s a lot easier to collect data than to collect understanding,” Ramakrishnan said. For example, it’s easier to provide a machine learning program with thousands of photos of animals and tell it which ones depict cats and which depict dogs, as opposed to trying to teach a program all the complicated ways a cat can be distinguished from a dog. Feeding the program labeled data helps it learn how to tell the difference between the two on its own.

Machine learning “makes decisions that generalize patterns that we would not have found otherwise,” Gupta said. “It’s as good as the data and the models that we have.”

Thus, machine learning is best suited for situations with lots of data — thousands or millions of examples, like recordings from conversations with customers, sensor logs from machines, or ATM transactions.

**What is generative AI?**
--------------------------

**Generative AI**is a newer type of machine learning that can create new content — including text, images, or videos — based on large datasets. **Large language models** —AI programs that can process and generate text — are a prominent type of generative AI. A hallmark iteration of generative AI, ChatGPT, was released by OpenAI in 2022 and quickly took off because of how well it was able to respond to user prompts written in plain language and then quickly generate new content. Other commonly used chatbots or LLMs include Anthropic’s Claude, Google’s Gemini, Microsoft’s Copilot, and Meta’s Llama, which have all been updated in the past year to provide more accurate results and be more responsive.

“Machine learning captures complex correlations and patterns in the data we have. Generative AI goes further,” Gupta said. Fine-tuned, specific generative AI models can identify relationships within traditional datasets that machine learning cannot. “That’s where the edge lies,” Gupta said.

Instead of making a prediction or identifying a pattern, generative AI creates new content —it can answer questions, compose emails, or brainstorm ideas, for example. “There are so many use cases for[GPT](https://stackademic.com/blog/understanding-the-difference-between-gpt-and-llm-a-comprehensive-comparison-1f624c713507) models these days,” Gupta said. “You see a lot of companies trying to find a way in which they can use them within their own frameworks, be it to transcribe calls in a call center, navigate policy documents, or help new employees learn the company’s existing software code.”

However, Gupta cautioned that companies developing or using generative AI or machine learning should be aware of potential issues, including [inaccuracies](https://mitsloanedtech.mit.edu/ai/basics/addressing-ai-hallucinations-and-bias/) and [bias.](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/ai-bias)

**Best use cases for generative AI**
------------------------------------

In addition to its main function, which is generating new content, generative AI is taking over tasks that traditional machine learning has historically performed. These situations include:

**When you’re dealing with everyday language or common images.**LLMs have been trained on a large amount of text or images and can be used “off the shelf” to classify and detect things.For example, a company might want to analyze online product reviews to identify user reports of product defects. This once meant building a machine learning model trained to identify such reviews —a process that takes effort, time, and money. Today a company can input product reviews into a LLM and ask it whether the dataset contains any product improvement insights, Ramakrishnan said.

GPT-4 and similar models “can be more accurate than a custom-built machine learning model, and you can get an application up and running much sooner,” he said.

Generative AI models are also[becoming more affordable](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/ai-report-highlights-smaller-better-cheaper-models/), Ramakrishnan noted, so over time, fewer companies will be priced out of using them.

**When you want a more accessible option.** Using generative AI models is something many software engineers can do without a large amount of extra training, whereas building machine learning models requires technical expertise. Generative AI “is a democratizing force in that sense. It makes it way more accessible,” Ramakrishnan said.

If a problem or opportunity is based on using everyday information, “try generative AI first,” he advised. “Don’t reflexively go back to machine learning like you used to.”

**When traditional machine learning is the better option**
----------------------------------------------------------

In some cases, though, machine learning is still the best option. Those situations could include:

**When you have privacy concerns.**You must exercise caution when feeding proprietary, sensitive, or confidential information into LLMs, because there is the potential for data leaks. And while it is possible to build your own private models, that requires specialist technical skills that may not be easily available in your organization. In these situations, you might want to stick to “the old-fashioned way,” Ramakrishnan said.

**When you’re using highly specific domain knowledge.** LLMs are trained on widely available data and suited to deal with everyday information. But they may not be as accurate for highly technical or niche tasks, like medical diagnoses based on MRI images. “If you are working on a domain-specific problem in which a lot of technical knowledge is required, a lot of jargon is involved, and the particular problem you’re working on is very particular to your company or your organization … you probably want to go the traditional [machine learning] route,” Ramakrishnan said —though he noted that generative AI models are improving rapidly, so that might change over time.

**When you already have a machine learning model.**Organizations have put a lot of effort into building machine learning programs for specific applications, like identifying potential fraud in credit card transactions. “There is probably not a huge urgency to rip them out and try to replace them with a generative AI system,” Ramakrishnan said. “The question is, what are the new use cases, the new things? That’s really where the decision point is going to come up.”

**When to use machine learning and generative AI together**
-----------------------------------------------------------

In several situations, machine learning and generative AI can be used together for better outcomes. These scenarios include the following:

**When you want to augment a machine learning model.**“Algorithms don’t have twenty-twenty vision of the world, and they’re as good as the models that we provide them. So if we can provide them [with] more context about the world using generative AI, then that only makes them better,” Gupta said.

She offered the example of a dataset containing people’s names, their heart rates, and the speed at which they have run. “A machine learning model will be able to predict information like the cardiac fitness of each person, cluster them into groups, or do a performance benchmarking,” Gupta said. “Generative AI-augmented machine learning might be able to squeeze a little bit more from the name of the person —inferring age and other demographics, using context external to this data.”

**When you want to easily design a machine learning model.**If you want to build a machine learning model, you can feed the data and instructions about desired function and techniques into a generative AI tool and ask it to build models, evaluate them on other datasets, and report on the accuracy of the models.

### Related Articles

[When humans and AI work best together](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/when-humans-and-ai-work-best-together-and-when-each-better-alone "When humans and AI work best together")[AI uses lots of data center energy — but there are solutions](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/ai-has-high-data-center-energy-costs-there-are-solutions "AI uses lots of data center energy — but there are solutions ")[How generative AI can boost highly skilled workers’ productivity](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/how-generative-ai-can-boost-highly-skilled-workers-productivity "How generative AI can boost highly skilled workers’ productivity")

Generative AI “is changing the life and workflow of machine learning people,” Ramakrishnan said, noting that the output of the models needs to be continually analyzed and critiqued to ensure that hallucination and errors aren’t compounded.

**When you want to generate data for a machine learning model.** In cases where you don’t have enough data to properly train a traditional machine learning model, generative AI can be used to create[synthetic data](https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/what-synthetic-data-and-how-can-it-help-you-competitively), which has the same statistical properties as a real-world dataset.

**When you want to prepare structured data for a machine learning model.** Tabular data in situations like industrial settings often contain errors, such as missing values, that need to be addressed before the data can be used to train a model. Rather than having to be cleaned up manually, the data can be uploaded to an LLM with a prompt to look for anomalies or mistakes.

“Generative AI makes the traditional machine learning workflow more efficient, all the way from data procurement to data cleaning to actually modeling,” Ramakrishnan said. “Every step of the process, you can use generative AI as sort of a turbocharger. But this is not a free lunch. The price you pay is the need to for constant vigilance to ensure that LLM-generated outputs are accurate.”

Given the variety of AI tools out there, deciding when to use what tool is becoming another skill AI practitioners need to have.

Ramakrishnan’s main takeaway: “If you want to generate stuff, use generative AI. If you want to predict things, but with everyday stuff, try generative AI first. If you want to predict things on domain-specific stuff, do predictive stuff, [use] traditional [machine learning]. It’s as simple as that.”

# What Is Generative AI? How It Works, Examples, Benefits, and Limitations

Written by Coursera Staff • Updated on

Generative AI is a popular technology that can quickly complete time-consuming tasks. Learn more about how it works, the benefits and limitations of AI generators, and jobs to explore if you're interested in this field.

Generative AI is a type of [artificial intelligence](https://www.coursera.org/articles/what-is-artificial-intelligence) tool that generates images, text, videos, and other media in response to inputted prompts from a user. AI generators, like [ChatGPT](https://www.coursera.org/articles/chatgpt) and DALL-E, have become popular for their ability to handle time-consuming tasks.

Learn about the definition of GenAI, how it differs from traditional AI, and the benefits and limitations of this new technology. Afterward, build your knowledge of GenAI with [DeepLearning.AI's Generative AI for Everyone](https://www.coursera.org/learn/generative-ai-for-everyone) course.

## What is generative AI?

Generative AI, commonly called GenAI, allows users to input a variety of [prompts](https://www.coursera.org/articles/what-is-prompt-engineering) to generate new content, such as text, images, videos, sounds, code, 3D designs, and other media. It is trained on documents and artifacts that already exist online, "learning" from these data sets so it can predict outcomes in the same ways humans might create on their own.

The rise of generative AI is largely due to the fact that people can use natural language to prompt AI now, so the [use cases](https://www.coursera.org/articles/generative-ai-use-cases) for it have multiplied. Across different industries, AI generators are now being used as a companion for writing, research, coding, designing, and more. And GenAI will continue to evolve as it's trained on more data.

### What's the difference between AI and generative AI?

Generative AI is a subset of artificial intelligence, which is essentially defined as the pursuit of creating machines capable of exhibiting (or exceeding) human intelligence. GenAI is a type of [machine learning](https://www.coursera.org/articles/what-is-machine-learning) focused on building generative models capable of producing a wide range of AI-generated content, including human-like text, images, and audio. So while AI is typically designed to perform a narrow range of tasks repetitively, GenAI can produce original content in response to various user inputs. Learn more about [the difference between AI and generative AI](https://www.coursera.org/articles/ai-vs-generative-ai).

## How does generative AI work?

Generative AI models generates new content by using [neural networks](https://www.coursera.org/articles/artificial-neural-network) to identify patterns in existing data. Trained on unsupervised and semi-supervised learning approaches, organizations can create foundation models from large, unlabeled data sets, essentially forming a base for AI systems to perform tasks [[1](https://encord.com/blog/foundation-models/)].

There are many [generative AI models](https://www.coursera.org/articles/generative-ai-models), including large language models (like ChatGPT), image generation models (like [DALL-E](https://www.coursera.org/articles/what-is-dall-e)), and audio generation models.

### Popular AI generators

There are several generative AI platforms you can become familiar with. You may find them helpful for automating certain processes in your workflow.

* **ChatGPT:** This language model has a foundation of GPT architecture that generates text that resembles something a human would produce. It's a helpful companion for research, strategy, and content creation.

* **DALL-E3:** This model generates images from text prompts, so creatives can create vibrant illustrations and concept art that’s a useful accompaniment to content marketing.

* **Microsoft Copilot:** This model, based on ChatGPT, is integrated into Microsoft's popular productivity suite of applications and is also available as a stand-alone product offering.

* **Google Gemini**: Google's answer to ChatGPT, Gemini is integrated into Google's own suite of productivity applications but is also accessible as a stand-alone chatbot.

## Generative AI examples

Use the examples below to understand the different ways you can use GenAI.

* Writing or improving content by producing a draft text in a specific style or length
* Adding subtitles or dubbing educational content, films, and other content in different languages
* Outlining briefs, resumes, term papers, and more
* Receiving a generic code to edit or improve upon
* Summarizing articles, emails, and reports
* Improving demonstration or explanation videos
* Creating music in a specific tone or style

Generative AI has many use cases that can benefit the way we work, by speeding up the content creation process or reducing the effort put into crafting an initial outline for a survey or email. However, generative AI also has limitations that may cause concern if it remains unregulated.

## Benefits and limitations of generative AI

As with any new technology, generative AI has benefits and limitations. For instance, while it can work across multiple languages, making it useful globally, it can also "hallucinate" answers and provide incorrect information. It's therefore important to understand [AI ethics](https://www.coursera.org/articles/generative-ai-ethics).

Let's review some of the other benefits and limitations to keep in mind as you use GenAI in your work.

### Benefits of GenAI

Some of the benefits of generative AI include:

* **Speed:** GenAI tools work quickly to complete tasks and generate content.

* **Multiple use cases:** GenAI can be used in several different situations, such as for coding or [writing a resume](https://www.coursera.org/articles/chatgpt-resume).

* **Scalable:** GenAI tools are often equipped to handle multiple users and tasks without degrading performance.

### Limitations of GenAI

Some of the limitations of generative AI include:

* **Requires human oversight and fact-checking:** Because GenAI can make mistakes, lacks a true understanding, and does not have genuine empathy, it requires humans to review its outputs.

* **Bias in training data:** AI systems learn from existing human-created content. If that content contains societal biases or prejudices, the AI can absorb and repeat them.

* **Privacy concerns:** There can be security risks. AI systems store user interactions and inputs, and sensitive personal or business information may be shared during conversations.

## Working in AI: GenAI opportunities

While GenAI is a technology that many professionals will need to learn to work with as more companies require the [AI skills](https://www.coursera.org/articles/generative-ai-skills) needed to do so, there are specific [roles for those interested in working in AI.](https://www.coursera.org/articles/generative-ai-roles) These opportunities are limited to highly technical programmers or engineers, either. There are [entry-level AI jobs](https://www.coursera.org/articles/entry-level-ai-jobs) to explore as well as more advanced jobs.

If you'd like to explore a career in GenAI, consider the following job titles:

**Technical GenAI roles:**

* [Machine learning engineer](https://www.coursera.org/articles/what-is-machine-learning-engineer)
* AI trainer
* [AI architect](https://www.coursera.org/articles/ai-architect)
* AI data scientist

**Business GenAI roles:**

1. AI product manager
2. AI implementation specialist
3. AI solutions architect
4. AI business analyst
5. AI ethics officer

**Creative GenAI roles:**

1. AI content strategist
2. AI writing specialist
3. AI content editor
4. AI UX designer

**Support GenAI roles:**

1. AI support specialist
2. AI training coordinator
3. AI quality assurance specialist
4. AI compliance manager
